kept.a:
Domaine Weinbach Sylvaner is the second pour of the dinner tasting’s wine pairing, served with the Tuna Crudo from November 2026.

It comes from Alsace, the wine region in the northeast of France that runs along the border with Germany. The grape is Sylvaner, a white grape, and the house’s pairing sheet describes this wine in one line: ripe pear with green notes and a lush texture. So expect ripe orchard fruit first, then something fresher and greener, in a wine that feels round in the mouth.

The sheet prints no vintage, so ask the sommelier which year is open before you name one at the table. It is a four ounce pour with the pairing and it is not on the by-the-glass list.

With the Tuna Crudo the ripe pear sits beside the carrot and the burnt orange, and the fresh green note suits the coriander.

Sell it as part of the pairing, not on its own: it is the second of five pours with the dinner tasting. Name the place and the grape, then give the guest the sheet’s three notes. Say: “Next is a Sylvaner from Domaine Weinbach in Alsace: ripe pear, a little green freshness and a lush texture.” If a guest asks for a glass outside the pairing, check with the sommelier first.

Asked: What is Sylvaner?

Answer: A white grape. This one is from Domaine Weinbach in Alsace, in northeastern France, and it shows ripe pear with green notes and a lush texture.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Our sheet says ripe pear and a lush texture and does not say dry or sweet, so ask the sommelier how the open bottle tastes before you answer.

Asked: What vintage is it?

Answer: The pairing sheet prints none. Ask the sommelier which year is open tonight.

The pairing sheet of 22 November 2026 prints no vintage: never name a year until the sommelier confirms the bottle open. It replaced the Fichet Mâcon-Igé as the second pour, so do not describe a Chardonnay with this course. It is a pairing pour and has no glass price. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Pour 4 oz as the second course lands, chilled, in a white-wine glass, label toward the guest. Say: “Sylvaner from Domaine Weinbach in Alsace, for your Tuna Crudo.” Clear the Champagne glass only when the guest has finished it. Confirm the vintage with the sommelier before service.

kept.a:
White Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the third pour of the dinner tasting’s wine pairing, served with the Fish Bouillabaisse from November 2026: the Domaine du Vieux Lazaret Blanc.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape is a village and an appellation in the Southern Rhône, in the south of France. Guests know it for red wine; white is the smaller part of what it makes. The house’s pairing sheet describes this one as a Grenache Blanc blend with notes of white flowers, lemon and apricot and a full-bodied texture. So it is a white with weight: floral on the nose, citrus and stone fruit on the palate, and round rather than sharp.

The sheet prints no vintage and does not name the other grapes, so ask the sommelier which year is open and what the blend is before you say either at the table. It is a four ounce pour with the pairing and it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Sell it as the surprise of the pairing: a white from a village guests know for red. It is the third of five pours with the dinner tasting, served with the Fish Bouillabaisse. Say: “This is a white Châteauneuf-du-Pape, a Grenache Blanc blend: white flowers, lemon and apricot, with real body.” A glass on its own is the sommelier’s call, so ask before you offer one.

Asked: I thought Châteauneuf-du-Pape was red?

Answer: Most of it is. The village also makes white wine in smaller amounts, and this is one: a Grenache Blanc blend from Domaine du Vieux Lazaret.

Asked: What does it taste like?

Answer: White flowers, lemon and apricot, with a full-bodied texture. It has more weight than a crisp white.

Asked: What grapes are in it?

Answer: Our sheet says a Grenache Blanc blend and names no other grape. Ask the sommelier for the rest of the blend.

The pairing sheet of 22 November 2026 prints no vintage and only part of the blend: never name a year or a second grape until the sommelier confirms them. It replaced the Louis Jadot Beaune, a red, as the third pour, so do not describe a Pinot Noir with this course. It is a pairing pour and has no glass price. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Pour 4 oz as the third course lands, cool rather than ice cold, in a larger white-wine glass, label toward the guest. Say: “A white Châteauneuf-du-Pape from Domaine du Vieux Lazaret, for your Fish Bouillabaisse.” Confirm the vintage and the glass with the sommelier before service.
